subject: Cooking
title: Types of Salt: Not All Crystals Are Equal
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Types of Salt: Not All Crystals Are Equal.

hook.text: A teaspoon of table salt and a teaspoon of flaky sea salt taste wildly different. Same mineral, different impact.

buildup.text: Table salt is finely ground with anti-caking agents. Each grain is dense and uniformly salty.

discovery.text: Flaky salt like Maldon has hollow pyramid crystals that crunch and dissolve slowly on the tongue.

twist.text: By weight, all salt is equally salty. By volume, flaky salt is less salty because crystals have air gaps.

climax.text: Chefs use kosher salt for cooking (even coverage) and finishing salt for texture and burst of flavor.

punchline.text: The right salt at the right time changes everything.

quiz.question: Why does a teaspoon of flaky salt taste less salty than table salt?
options: Hollow crystals create air gaps reducing density

details.summary: Salt crystal size and shape dramatically affect cooking results. Flaky Maldon dissolves instantly for finishing. Coarse kosher salt is easy to pinch for seasoning. Fine table salt is dense and easy to oversalt with. Diamond Crystal kosher salt measures half the salinity of Morton's by volume.
details.whyItMatters: Two brands of kosher salt differ by nearly two to one in salinity per volume. Not knowing this is the most common cause of under- or over-seasoned food in recipe translation.
takeaways: Crystal shape determines how much salt fits in a measuring spoon
Diamond Crystal is roughly half as salty per volume as Morton's
Finishing salts add texture and visual appeal, not just flavor

faq.question: Why do professional chefs prefer kosher salt?
faq.answer: Kosher salt's large crystals are easy to pinch and distribute evenly. You can feel the amount between your fingers. It dissolves at a moderate rate, giving control during seasoning. It lacks the metallic taste of iodized table salt's anti-caking agents.

faq.question: What are finishing salts used for?
faq.answer: Finishing salts like Maldon flakes and fleur de sel are added just before serving for crunch, visual appeal, and bursts of salinity. Their large crystals do not fully dissolve, providing texture contrast.
